topicTitle: Web Security Architecture (XSS, CSRF, CORS, CSP)

lessons.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Prevention & DOM Sanitization (DOMPurify)
lessons.description: XSS attacks inject malicious scripts into your pages — learn to prevent them with input sanitization and output encoding.

sections.heading: What is XSS?
paragraphs: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) allows attackers to inject malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users. It's one of the most common web vulnerabilities.
list: Stored XSS — malicious script saved on the server (e.g., in comments)
Reflected XSS — script reflected in URL parameters
DOM-based XSS — script injected via client-side DOM manipulation
Prevention: never use innerHTML with user input, sanitize everything

codeExamples.heading: XSS prevention techniques
explanation: innerHTML with user input is the #1 cause of XSS vulnerabilities.
textContent is always safe — it escapes HTML automatically.
DOMPurify removes dangerous elements and attributes from HTML.
Always sanitize before using innerHTML with untrusted content.

practice.task: Create a comment system that safely displays user input. Test with malicious HTML input and verify it's sanitized.
hints: Use textContent or DOMPurify to sanitize input.

keyTakeaways: XSS injects malicious scripts into your pages through user input.
Never use innerHTML with unsanitized user input.
Use textContent for plain text, DOMPurify for HTML.
Always validate and sanitize input on both client and server.
lessons.challenge: Build a rich text editor that allows safe HTML formatting while preventing XSS attacks.

lessons.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Mitigation Strategies
lessons.description: CSRF tricks authenticated users into performing unwanted actions — defend with tokens and SameSite cookies.

sections.heading: What is CSRF?
paragraphs: CSRF forces an authenticated user's browser to send requests to a site where they're logged in. The browser automatically includes cookies, so the request appears legitimate.
list: Attacker creates a form that submits to your site
User's browser sends cookies automatically with the request
Server can't tell the difference between legitimate and forged requests
Defense: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, checking Origin/Referer

codeExamples.heading: CSRF prevention
explanation: CSRF tokens are unique per session — embedded in forms and verified on submission.
SameSite cookies prevent the browser from sending cookies on cross-site requests.
Checking Origin/Referer headers verifies the request came from your site.
Use multiple defenses together for robust protection.

practice.task: Implement CSRF protection on a POST endpoint using a random token embedded in a form and verified on submission.
hints: Store in session and embed in a hidden form field.

keyTakeaways: CSRF tricks authenticated users into performing unwanted actions.
CSRF tokens verify that requests originate from your own forms.
SameSite cookies prevent cross-site cookie transmission.
lessons.challenge: Build a complete CSRF protection system with token generation, form embedding and server-side verification.

lessons.title: Configuring CORS Headers & Content Security Policy (CSP) Directives
lessons.description: Control which origins can access your API and what resources your pages can load.

sections.heading: CORS and CSP
list: CORS — controls which origins can make requests to your API
CSP — controls which resources (scripts, styles, images) your pages can load

codeExamples.heading: CORS and CSP configuration
explanation: CORS restricts which origins can access your API.
Allow specific origins — never use * in production.
CSP restricts what resources pages can load.
CSP prevents XSS by blocking unauthorized script sources.

practice.task: Configure CORS to allow requests from a specific origin and set a CSP header that only allows scripts from your own domain.
hints: CSP: script-src 'self' blocks inline and external scripts.
Test with a script from a different origin — it should be blocked.

keyTakeaways: CORS controls which origins can access your API.
CSP controls which resources your pages can load.
CSP is a powerful defense against XSS — configure it carefully.
lessons.challenge: Set up a complete security headers configuration including CORS, CSP, HSTS and X-Frame-Options.
